concept.name: Tom-next swap
concept.definition: A short-dated FX swap used to roll a currency position forward by one day: the holder buys (or sells) a foreign currency amount settling tomorrow and simultaneously does the opposite transaction settling the day after (the spot value date). Institutions use tom-next swaps at the end of each day to close out and re-institute foreign balances, thereby collecting or paying the overnight interest differential (cost of carry) without holding an open FX position.
concept.intuition: Tom-next is the daily 'roll' that keeps a spot FX position from ever settling, in exchange for paying or receiving one day of the interest-rate gap.
concept.mechanics: The near leg settles on the tomorrow date (T+1) and the far leg on the spot date (T+2), shifting the position's value date by one day. The price, in swap points, reflects the one-day interest rate differential between the two currencies (with extra days priced over weekends and holidays); retail platforms implement the same economics as the daily rollover or swap charge on open positions.
concept.formula: Tom-next swap points ~ S x (r_q - r_b) x (days / 360 or 365 by convention), where S = spot rate and r_q, r_b = quote- and base-currency overnight rates.
concept.failure_modes: Tom-next pricing turns on overnight rates and day counts, so costs jump over weekends (three days) and quarter/ year-ends when funding rates spike; traders ignoring the roll can see carry economics dominate returns on long-held leveraged positions.
concept.misconceptions: A tom-next roll is not a new directional trade and not a fee set arbitrarily by the broker — it is the market-priced interest differential for deferring settlement by one day.
concept.example: A desk long EUR/USD over value date Tuesday executes a tom-next swap: it sells EUR settling Wednesday and buys it back settling Thursday, paying or earning one day of the EUR-USD rate differential.
